Vs.

full_judgment:
SAN Mominur Rahman J : This Miscellaneous Appeal under section 48 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 has been preferred being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order dated 23-8-2006 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 790 of 2006 dismissing the case on contest. 

 2. The Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 790 of 2006 arises out of an application filed under section 42(1) of the Arbitration Act by the appellant hereof for setting aside the arbitral award passed on 3-6-2006 in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 12 of 2005 by the Arbitral Tribunal consisting of Mr Justice Latifur Rahman as Chairman and Messrs Justice Md Abdur Rouf and Justice AKM Sadeque, as Arbitrators. The Arbitration was constituted by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, on an application filed by the respondent-contractor for appointment of an arbitration, registered as Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 2005, and, on hearing the parties the Court appointed Mr Justice Md Abdur Rouf and Mr Justice AKM Sadeque as arbitrators, who subsequently appointed Mr Justice Latifur Rahman as Chairman, and which was approved by the learned District Judge, Dhaka. 

 3. In the Arbitration case before the Arbitral Tribunal, hereinafter referred to as the Tribunal, the respondent hereof submitted its statement of claims for Taka 97,72,74,639.88 paisa on different accounts because of the inordinate delay in completing the Project for which the employer-appellants were found to be responsible. Because of delay the respondent-contractors have to make excess and extra- payments on the following heads of account: (i) for the contracted works done after the stipulated period; (ii) for works done beyond the contract schedule i.e. non-scheduled and non-tendered work items at the instance of the employer appellant; (iii) for rents required to be paid for keeping and maintaining the machineries and equipment as well as for the storage site for the period beyond the contract period; (iv) for payment for excess administrative expenses i.e. maintaining office and staff for the period beyond the contract period; (v) for excess bank interest and other charges required to be paid to the Bank for the period beyond the contract period; and (vi) for damages for loss in business and goodwill. The appellants hereof submitted the statement of defence denying the claim of the respondent hereof. Both the parties, accepting the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, contested the case. 

 4. The Tribunal, on consideration of the materials and evidences on record, on physical verification and the submissions of the learned Advocates of the parties, found that the Arbitration Case arose out of the contract between the parties for construction of CW Pump House with some auxiliary structures (Lot-2) of 210 MW Siddhirganj Thermal Power Station Construction Project at Siddhirganj, District- Narayanganj, hereinafter referred to as the Project, under agreement No.3 18/Lot- 2/99/180 dated 30-12- 1999, hereinafter referred to as the Contract, which, amongst others, contains an arbitration clause, and that Project was to be completed within 365 days from the date of Contract and that the respondent- contractor had to furnish a performance bank guarantee for Taka 49,19,602.00 vide Performance Bank Guarantee No.99/68 dated 3-11-1999 issued by Rupali Bank Ltd., local office, and that the respondent-contractors completed the Project on 30-8-2004. The Project could be completed in 1706 days in place of contract period of365 days because of delay caused due to fault of the appellant-employers, resulting in excess payments required to be paid by the respondent-contractors on account of the work-items done to complete the project, for the period beyond the contract period; (ii) the Non- tendered and Non-scheduled work items done at the instance of the appellants; (iii) maintaining the administrative office with staff, etc. for the period beyond the contract period; (iv) rents for keeping the machineries and equipment, and storage site therefor  for the period beyond the contract period; (v) Bank interest and charges paid to the Bank for the period beyond the stipulated Contract period; as well as (vi) damages and compensation for the loss in business and goodwill. The Tribunal on detailed discussions found the appellants responsible for the delay in completing the Project, which fact has been admitted by the Power Development Board itself in its 1071st and 1078th meetings held on 22-12-2003 and 9-2-2004 respectively, and accordingly, accepted that the respondents hereof are entitled to compensation and enhancement of rates of work done for the delay. The Tribunal considering the materials and evidences on record and the submissions of the learned Advocates of the contesting parties found that there was delay of 1341 days beyond the contract period of 365 days and accordingly, gave the award in favour of the respondent-contractors for (i) Taka 7,70,67,580.30 paisa as against the claim of Taka 36,12,95,291.73 pasia on the account of works done beyond the stipulated period mentioned in the contract; and (ii) Taka 26,33,72,400 as against the claim of Taka 30,44,20,000; on account of extra and excess amount of rent paid for keeping and maintaining the machineries and equipment as well the storage site for the period beyond the stipulated contract period; and (iii) Taka 1,04,06,160 paisa as against the claim for Taka 4,34,31,000 paisa for keeping the administrative section i.e. for maintaining the office, staff and stationery etc., required for completing the project, and for the period beyond the stipulated contract period and (iv) Taka 4,45,84,167 as against the claim of Taka 5,00,00,000; paid to the Bank on account of bank interest and other charges, for the period beyond the stipulated contract period. The claim on account of damages for loss in business and goodwill amounting to Taka 9,00,00,000 and the claim of Taka 12,81,27,674.15 for Non-tendered and Non-schedule items were totally rejected. Thus, the total amount as awarded stands at Taka 39,54,30,307.30 paisa as against the total claim of Taka 97,72,74,639 paisa. The Tribunal awarded interest @ 15% per annum with effect from 30-3-2005 to 3-6-2006 and allowed further interest @ 15% per annum from the date of the award till realisation of the award amount. 

 5. The employer appellants being aggrieved by the award given by the Arbitral Tribunal preferred Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.790 of 2006 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka, as per section 42(1) of the Arbitration Act, 2001, challenging the sward on as many as 12 counts. The application filed under section 42(1) of the Arbitration Act, 2001, has been registered as Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.790 of 2006. The respondent- contractors hereof as opposite party filed a written objection and that the learned District Judge relying on section 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 rejected the Miscellaneous Case observing, amongst others, that the grounds taken for setting aside the award have no relevance with the grounds mentioned in section 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, inasmuch as the Court is to decide the case on the grounds mentioned in section 43 in reference. 

 6. Being aggrieved there against, the appellants have come up with the instant appeal with as many as eleven (11) grounds, which are to the effect, that the learned District Judge, Dhaka, totally misread and misapplied section 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001; and that the Tribunal's decision is hit by section 43(1)(b )(ii) of the Arbitration Act, 2001 being opposed to law; and that the Tribunal allowed the claim on the account of payment of interest without being satisfied but on mere assumption; and that the Arbitral Tribunal, in gross violation of the contractual provisions, allowed the claim on the count of administrative expenses ignoring the rules of evidence; and that the Tribunal in gross violation of the Contract allowed the enhancement in the rates of works done during the period beyond the stipulated contract period, including the non-tendered and non-scheduled work items; and that the Tribunal did not consider that the respondent-contractors failed to take step to mitigate the losses; and that the learned District Judge, Dhaka, came to an erroneous conclusion in not considering the materials on record and not considering that the grounds taken by the appellants, in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 790 of 2006 which attracts section 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, and thus arrived at an erroneous decision. 

 7. Mr Tufailur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the appellant-petitioner, who also appeared for the appellants before the Tribunal, submitted that the amounts awarded are excessive in nature and beyond the terms of the Contract; and that the learned District Judge, Dhaka, failed to consider the grounds set forth in the application filed under section 42(1) of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and most illegally rejected the miscellaneous case without entering into the merit of the case and thereby acted illegally in dismissing the case. 

 8. With our consent, Mr Abdur Razzaq, learned Advocate, also made submissions on behalf of the appellants, and referring to section 43(1)(b )(ii) of the Arbitration Act, 2001 submitted that the Arbitral Award under challenge is prima facie opposed to the law now in force in Bangladesh as is evident from the materials and evidences on record, and that the learned District Judge failed to consider the same, inasmuch as the award as given is hit by section 73 of the Contract Act and therefore, is opposed to law for the time being in force and consequently, attracts section 43(1 )(b )(ii) of the Arbitration Act, 2001, thereby the rejection of the case holding that the grounds set forth do not attract section 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 is not correct., The learned Advocate in elaborating his submissions submitted that the learned District Judge failed to consider that the award amount as given is unreasonably at the higher side and that the respondent-contractors failed to take steps for mitigating the losses and that the compensation/ damages as claimed do not arise in the usual course of the breach as to delay and it could not be known to the parties whether such compensation/damages are likely to be the result of such delay and that the bank interest as awarded is against the provisions of the Contract. The learned Advocate also submitted that the compensation amount for the delay as awarded is excessive and not reasonable. Learned Advocate lastly submitted that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon the Arbitration, inasmuch as the respondent contractors have no locus standi to proceed with the Arbitration not being a direct party to the Contract. Learned Advocate referring to some decisions of the Indian Jurisdiction i.e. in the case of (i) Karsandas H Thacker vs Saran Engineering Co Ltd reported in AIR 1965 SC 1981 and (ii) Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. vs Saw Pipes LId. reported in AIR 2003 SC 2629, which are on section 73 of the Contract Act, submitted that section 73 of the Indian Contract Act and section 73 of our Contract Act are same. The case reported in AIR 1982 SC 1981 relates to an illustration to the effect, that a person at fault in respect of a contract for supply of goods has to pay the price difference only and is not liable to pay any compensation, which the non-defaulter party is required to pay to the 3rd party in fulfilling the contract, since necessity of such payment made to 3rd party could not be known to the defaulting party when the contract was entered into, and that the necessity for payment made to the 3rd party did not arise in the usual course of the breach of the contract and was not likely to be the result of the breach of the contract. The case reported in AIR 2003 SC 2629 refers to compensation paid for breach of contract as per sections 73 and 74 of the Indian Contract Act and· the same relates to jurisdiction of the Court to award compensation in case of contract for supply of goods by purchase, which was unqualified expenses and was unreasonable; and that the party put to suffer by the purchase of the contracted goods is entitled to reasonable compensation for any loss suffered by him due to breach of contract, provided the party when entered into the contract was likely to know that compensation was required to be paid for such breach. The aforesaid decisions have been placed in support of the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the appellants to the effect that the appellants had no knowledge or was aware that if there be any delay in completing the project the respondent contractors would be required to pay extra amounts towards damage or compensation or excess rents to the owners of the machinery and the equipment as well as for the storage site, and the man- power engaged in completing the project for the period beyond the contract period; and for maintaining the office with staff, etc. for the period beyond the contract period, as claimed, and therefore, such claims do not attract section 73 of the Contract Act and hence the award is illegal. 

 9. The learned Advocate, on the issue of jurisdiction of the Arbitral Tribunal to proceed with the arbitration, submitted that in the Contract the respondent is not a party, but is the Attorney of the Contractors named in the Contract, and, as such, they cannot initiate and or proceed with this arbitration. The learned Advocate also referring to section 2(c) of the Arbitration Act, 2001 submitted that one of the partners of the joint venture contractors being a foreigner, the arbitration has become an International Commercial Arbitration and therefore, the learned District Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the application under section 12(4) of the Arbitration Act, 2001, for the appointment of arbitrators, since in case of International Commerce Arbitration the appointment of arbitrators is to be made by the Chief Justice or by any other Judge of the Supreme Court designated by the Chief Justice; and thus, the Arbitral Tribunal formed by the learned District Judge is without jurisdiction and not valid, consequently, the award is also illegal. 

 10. The learned Advocate appearing for the respondent-contractors submitted that the appeal as filed is liable to be dismissed as there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge, inasmuch as the grounds set forth in the application for setting aside the award submitted before the learned District Judge, under section 42(1) of the Act, do not attract the grounds mentioned in said section 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and accordingly, the Court below has rightly rejected the prayer for setting aside the award The learned Advocate further submitted that the present Arbitration Act, 2001 has been made taking into consideration of the fact that the defaulting party in a contract taking advantage of the provisions of the earlier law used to delay the implementation of the award, although the object of an arbitration is to give speedy relief avoiding the normal legal procedures. In the instant case, the Arbitral Tribunal was formed through the Court of law in participation of the appellants, and the appellants accepted the arbitrators and accordingly, surrendering to the Arbitral Tribunal contested the arbitration, without raising any objection against the jurisdiction of the Tribunal or the arbitration and that on due consideration of the facts said circumstances and the materials on record as well as the submission made by the learned Advocates of the respective parties, the award has been given and that the Arbitral Tribunal in coming to its decision has considered all the items referred to in the statement of claims as well as the objection raised thereagainst in the statement of defence and that relying on the proceedings of the 1071st and 1078th Board Meetings of the appellant No.1, the Tribunal found that the appellants are responsible for the delay in completing the project and the appellants have admitted that the respondent- contractors are entitled to compensation and enhancements in the rates for the work items and for compensation; and therefore, there is no illegality in the award. The learned Advocate also submitted that the Tribunal has given due consideration in assessing the award amounts, required to be paid by the contractors to the Bank on account of the bank interest and charges, etc arid the expenses incurred for maintaining the Administrative officers, staffs, etc as well as for paying extra rents on account of the machinery and equipment and the storage site, both items for the period beyond the stipulated contract period, and that the award amount given is far less than the actual i.e. claimed amount. The claims were supported by materials on record. It has been asserted that the office and staff, etc and the machinery/equipment, etc. are required to be kept till completing the project, to comply with the condition set forth in the Contract. In the instant case, the claimed amount was Taka 97,72,74,639.88 paisa whereas the award has been given for Taka 39,54,30,307.30 paisa only. The award amount is around 40% of the claimed amount, which, ex-facie, is not sufficient but to avoid further damage and loss the respondent-contractor accepted the award. The learned Advocate relying on the case of Sonali Bank vs Karnaphuli Works Ltd decided by the Appellate Division vide judgment and order dated 22-11-1993, reported in 46 DLR (AD) 55 submitted that the Court is not prevented from adopting the method 'for determining the amount of compensation as per the bank rate prevalent at the relevant time after hearing the parties and that section- 73 of the Contract Act provides for compensation for loss or damages caused by the breach in the contract. However, such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained because of any breach. In the instant case, the compensations given were neither remote nor indirect but are directly relevant since extra and excess amounts were required to be paid because of the delay in completing the project. It is known to all concerned in the instant case that the administrative office with manpower, etc and the rented machinery and equipment with storage site had to be maintained till completion of the project as per terms of the Contract. Further, in the instant project, the office and its employees and the machinery and equipment were brought as per requirement of the appellants and required to be kept in terms of the Contract and were within the knowledge of the employer-appellants and the same could not be released or reduced prior to completion of the project, since both items were necessary for completion of the project. Learned Advocate also submitted that in the Contract there is condition set forth for penalty in case of any fault on the part of the respondent contractors and that the fact remains that the appellants being satisfied with the works of the respondent-contractors and having found no fault on the part of the respondent contractors paid the bills and accepted the project without objection. 

 11. The learned Advocate referring to section Q of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and the copy of the proceedings of the appellants' Board Meeting Nos. 1071st and 1078th , produced before the Tribunal and kept with the records of the case, submitted that the objection as to the locus standi of the respondent is not maintainable, inasmuch as the appellants have accepted the respondent contractor as the contractors and that the fact remains that the tender offer was submitted in the name of the joint venture association namely "Arab Contractors-Shah Islam Joint Venture" and subsequently, the said association was converted into a Bangladesh company, limited by shares, incorporated under the Companies Act of Bangladesh, namely Arab Contractors (BD) Ltd, with consent of the employer-appellants, and the company has been admittedly, accepted by the appellants as contractors for all purposes without any objection and further, this objection was not pressed at the time of appointment of the Arbitral Tribunal by the Court or during the proceedings of the arbitration and also, not pressed before the learned District Judge, before whom the application for setting aside the award was made and thus the appellants are barred by the principle of waiver, acquiescence and estoppel from raising such objection. Section 6 of the Arbitration Act provides that any right under the Contract if not pressed and the party proceeds with the arbitration it shall be deemed that the concerned party has waived such right. Learned Advocate also submits that the appellants for all practical purposes accepted the respondent as the contractors and made all correspondences and dealt with said respondent-contractors, including payment of the bills without objection. 

 12. Learned Advocate taking us through section 2( c) of the Arbitration Act submitted that the International Commercial Arbitration means an arbitration in which one of the parties, (i) if individual, is a national or habitually resident in any foreign country; or (ii) if a body corporate, is incorporated in any foreign country; or (iii) if is a company or association or a body of individuals, whose "Central Management and Control" is exercised from any country other than Bangladesh; whereas in the instant case, the Joint Venture in reference had its "Central Management and Control" in Bangladesh and subsequently, the said joint venture association having been converted into a limited company, incorporated under Company Laws of Bangladesh, became a Bangladeshi juristic person, hence the arbitration in reference cannot be treated as an International Commercial Arbitration as submitted by the learned Advocate for the appellants. There- fore, the objection raised as to jurisdiction of the learned District Judge, Dhaka in making the appointment of the Arbitral Tribunal is misconceived and not tenable in the eye of law. 

 13. The learned Advocate for the respondent- contractors, taking us through the provisions of section 73 of the Contract Act, submitted that in the instant case, the award as given as to the rate or enhanced rate for the work items including non- tendered and non-scheduled and extra works, required to be done by the respondent contractors at the instance of the appellants do not attract section 73 of the Contract Act, inasmuch as it cannot be said that an award given as compensation or enhancement of the rates or fixing of rate for the non- tendered and non-scheduled items in a contract for construction work, in case of delay caused by the employer, is unknown and or do not naturally arise in usual course or not likely to be a result of such delay. The learned Advocate submitted that in the instant case, the award on account of bank interest and charges, the maintenance costs and expenses for the office, its employees and ancillary items, etc and the rents for the machinery/equipment and the storage site for the period beyond the Contract period has been allowed since such payments were required to be made for the extra-period involved, due to the delay caused by the employer-appellants and award of such compensation is well known in the field of contracts for construction works, inasmuch as in case of construction projects, time is treated as an essence of the contract. The learned Advocate lastly submitted that in the instant case there was no scope for taking steps to mitigate the loss, inasmuch as the appellants being admittedly responsible for the delay and that the maintenance of the office with its employees and other necessities as well as the machinery and equipment at the storage, site, till completion of the project, is a requirement of the terms of the Contract, and that the project could not be completed without those factors. 

 14. We have perused the materials on record and considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of the contesting parties. It appears that the application for setting aside the award as made under section 42(1) of the Arbitration Act, 2001, registered as Miscellaneous Arbitration Case No. 790/2006, has been rejected by the learned District Judge observing that the grounds set forth therein were not in the form as required, section 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. However, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant has submitted that the learned District Judge did not consider the pro- visions of section 43(1)(b )(ii), which reads as under: 

 (b) The Court or the High Court Division, as the case may be, is satisfied that: 

 The learned Advocate for the appellants asserted that the Arbitral' award Was opposed to section 73 of the Contract Act and thus opposed to a law in force in Bangladesh i.e. section 43 (1)(b )(ii) of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and that in the award the compensation or loss as given in respect of the claims on account of bank interest and charges as well as rents for machinery and equipment and the storage site would not naturally arise in usual course and that the appellant did not have any reason to know that such breach of delay would occur and that the respondent-contractors would be required to make excess payments on account of rents for keeping the machineries and equipment beyond the stipulated contract period and to pay extra bank interests and charges against the performance bank guarantee, etc to the bank for the period beyond the Contract period. It is to be noted that in the instant case that the Tribunal did not allow the claim of the respondent on account of the "damages and losses for business and goodwill". In the instant case, as the delay in completing the project is admittedly a breach of Contract and the appellants were held responsible for the delay, hence the consequential compensation and payments have to be borne by the appellants. The responsibility for the delay has been admitted by the appellants, as the appellant No. 1 in its 1071st and 1078th Board meetings, taking legal advisers' opinion into consideration, and also held that the contractors are entitled to the enhancement of rates in carrying out the work items for the period beyond the contract period. However, in the said meetings the amounts for compensation or enhancement of rates were not decided. 

 15. It is the settled principle of law that the Court will not interfere with the amount awarded by any arbitration provided the same is not against any law in force or ex facie too excessive and unreasonable. The Court may interfere with any award given by an arbitration, if found to have acted against any law or acted malafide or did not consider any material evidence substantially affecting the award amount or that award as given is without any basis. However after the promulgation of the present Arbitration Act, 2001 the award can only be set aside, if the grounds set forth in the application filed under section 42(1) of the said Act are in conformity with section 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. In a case of contract for construction works it is natural that the question of delay is regarded as a major issue, inasmuch the time factor is treated as an essence of such contract. The learned Advocate for the respondent contractors asserted that the appellants had the power to levy penalty on the respondent-contractors if there be any delay or fault otherwise on their part in completing the project. No allegation of any fault has been made against the respondent-contractor in the completion of the project. Rather, it appears that the appellants accepted their own fault for the delay and also admitted that the contractors are entitled to get enhanced rates for the works done beyond the contract period. The interest has been given complying with the provisions of section 38 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. 

 16. Considering the aforesaid facts and the provisions of laws, we are of the view that in the instant case, the provisions of section 73 of the Contract Act do not apply. Thus the objection as raised relying on section 43(1)(b )(ii) has no substance in the instant case. 

 18. The First Miscellaneous Appeal is accordingly, dismissed with cost of Taka 50,000. The appellants are directed to satisfy the award within 45 working days.
